questions.q: A classmate sums up the study: 'There are three spheres: an invisible one, a visible one and a solid one.' Say what is right and what is wrong in that summary. For each station, say what its script makes that the station before it does not, and what all three scripts share. Then say what the first station shows that the other two could not show on their own.
questions.rubric: FULL: finds both errors. (1) The first station holds no sphere, invisible or otherwise. Its script only defines a position value: nothing is made or placed there, and the feeler crosses an empty place. A position is not the object placed at it. (2) The third station is not 'solid instead of visible'. Its script makes the same visible marker as the second and then adds a boundary (a physics body with a collision shape). The layers add up; they do not replace each other. What is right: only the second and third can be seen, and only the third stops the feeler. Each station adds one layer: first a value; then a surface (a mesh shown by a node placed at that value); then a boundary at the same value. All three scripts start from the same position value. The first station shows that a value alone gives nothing to see and nothing to meet, so the surface and the boundary are each something added to a place, not the place itself. HALF: finds one of the two errors but not the other. Or gives the three layers correctly but says nothing about what the first station shows. MAY LEAVE OUT: class names, file names, numbers, the words 'baseline' or 'control'. NOT SCORED: whether the student notes that the stations themselves stand apart in the room. WRONG: agreeing that the first station holds an invisible sphere or point; 'the third is a heavier, denser or different-material sphere'; 'the three stations sit at three different heights'; 'the first station is broken or unfinished'.

questions.q: In position.gd a classmate changes 1.12 to 1.7 and runs the study. Nothing appears at that station. They conclude either that the edit did not take effect or that something in the project is hiding the point. In visible.gd, the same change to the same line makes the white sphere rise. Explain why one edit shows nothing in one script and moves a sphere in the other. How sure can you be that the classmate's edit did take effect, and on what grounds?
questions.rubric: FULL: the line defines a value and nothing more: a Vector3 (three numbers held as one value) named point_position. A value is not an object; on its own it puts nothing in the scene. In visible.gd, other lines use that value: they make a node that displays a surface, give it the sphere mesh, place it at the value (marker.position = point_position) and join it to the station (add_child). So changing the value moves what is placed there. In position.gd nothing uses the value, so changing it changes nothing anyone can see. Certainty is high, and the grounds are reading: those few lines are the whole of position.gd, so nothing in it makes or places anything, and there is nothing to hide. Running agrees: nothing appears, whatever the value. The editor's unused-variable warning, if mentioned, says the same (defined, never used). HALF: says 'nothing uses the value' but cannot say what in visible.gd uses it. Or explains visible.gd correctly but gives no grounds for certainty. Or rests certainty on the run alone ('nothing appeared'), which cannot tell a failed edit from a hidden point. MAY LEAVE OUT: exact class names, if each role is clear; the warning. WRONG: 'save or restart the editor'; '1.7 puts the point out of view'; 'the feeler or the camera hides it'; 'a Vector3 should draw a dot'; 'position.gd needs a StaticBody3D before anything can be seen' (mixes up boundary and surface).

questions.q: Here are three one-line edits. Try each one alone, on the original scripts. For each, predict what you see at that station and what its feeler does, and say why. (a) In visible.gd, delete add_child(marker). (b) In visible.gd, delete marker.mesh = sphere. (c) In solid.gd, change solid.add_child(collider) to add_child(collider).
questions.rubric: FULL (all three predicted, each with its reason): (a) Nothing is visible. The marker still exists, with its surface and its position, but it is never joined to the station, so it is not part of the running scene. The feeler crosses, as before. (b) Nothing is visible. The node is placed and joined, but it was never given a surface to display: the sphere mesh exists, but no node shows it. The feeler crosses. (c) The white sphere still shows, because the marker is untouched, but now the feeler crosses. The collision shape no longer belongs to the body, so the body has no boundary. The station it now hangs from is a plain Node3D, not a physics body, so the shape gives the station no boundary either. A plus: noticing that the shape now also sits at the station's origin, at floor level, because only the body was placed at point_position. The common point: a part takes effect only when it is joined to what uses it. HALF: two of the three with reasons. Or all three predictions right but no reasons. Or (c) explained only by the shape's new location, without seeing that a shape works only as part of a body. MAY LEAVE OUT: editor warnings, exact class names. WRONG: (a) 'the sphere appears at the station's floor or origin'; (b) 'a default or grey sphere appears'; (c) 'nothing changes because the collider is still in the scene', 'the feeler now stops lower or somewhere else', or 'the white sphere disappears'.

questions.q: The study shows three stations: one where nothing can be seen and nothing stops the feeler; one where something can be seen but nothing stops it; and one where both hold. One combination is missing. Name it. Then change solid.gd so that its station shows the missing combination. Give the changed script, or the exact edits, and say what you expect to see when the study runs.
questions.rubric: Naming the combination carries little weight, because the three combinations listed give it away. The code and the prediction carry the score. FULL: the missing combination is a point that stops the feeler but cannot be seen (a boundary with no surface). The code keeps: point_position and radius; the StaticBody3D placed at point_position; the SphereShape3D given the radius; the CollisionShape3D given that shape; the collider joined to the body; and the body joined to the station. It removes the visible part: the whole marker block (keeping var radius), or only add_child(marker), or only marker.mesh = sphere. Expected: nothing visible at the third station, but its feeler stops in empty air where the sphere used to be. ACCEPT: any other way of leaving the marker unseen (for example marker.visible = false), if the student says why the boundary remains. HALF: the right combination, but the code breaks the boundary. For example, it deletes var radius or point_position, which the body still uses, or it drops add_child(solid) or solid.add_child(collider). Or the code is right but the prediction is wrong. MAY LEAVE OUT: the contact label's text, any numbers. WRONG: removing the body and keeping the marker (that rebuilds the second station); 'turn the light off to make it invisible'; 'a body with no visible surface cannot collide'.

questions.q: Change solid.gd so that the boundary is always a little larger than the visible sphere, by the same margin, whatever value you later give radius. Show the changed line or lines. Then change var radius := 0.14 to var radius := 0.28 and run. Predict what happens to the sphere's centre, to its visible size and to where the feeler stops. Explain why that one edit now resizes both the surface and the boundary.
questions.rubric: FULL: the boundary line becomes sphere_shape.radius = radius + m, for some small positive margin m (for example radius + 0.05), and the visible lines still read radius. With radius at 0.28: the centre stays at point_position, because radius sets size, not place. The surface grows around that same centre. The boundary grows with it and stays m beyond the surface. The feeler stops a little before the white surface, earlier than before, leaving a thin gap of air. Why: both radii are read from the one variable, so the script alone links surface and boundary. Keeping the variable in the boundary's line keeps that link; a fixed number would cut it. ACCEPT: shrinking the visible side instead (sphere.radius = radius - m, with sphere.height kept at twice that value), since the boundary still stays m larger. If sphere.height is left at radius * 2.0, the visible sphere is stretched: HALF. HALF: a fixed number (for example 0.19) that works for 0.14 but not for any value. Or radius * factor, which gives a proportional margin rather than the same one. Or correct code with a prediction that the sphere moves or rises. Or no account of why one edit resizes both. MAY LEAVE OUT: the exact margin, the size of the gap. WRONG: changing point_position; 'the boundary follows the visible sphere on its own'; 'the feeler stops exactly at the surface'.

questions.q: When the study runs, the second and third spheres look the same. What grounds do you have for saying that one is solid and the other is not? Take each kind of evidence in turn: looking, running the study, reading the two scripts, and changing a line and running again. For each, say what it can establish and what it cannot. Then a doubter says that the feeler test simply stops at whichever station is called Solid. Which evidence answers the doubter, and how?
questions.rubric: FULL: Looking cannot decide it. Both show the same surface, and a visible surface of any size gives nothing to collide with. Running shows a difference (one feeler crosses, the other stops) but not its cause. Reading shows what the scripts build: solid.gd makes the same marker and then a static body with a collision shape attached, at the same position; visible.gd makes only the marker. Each script is complete, so nothing else in it adds a boundary. Reading cannot show that the test responds to what was built. Changing a line and running again ties the two together: changing only the boundary's radius in solid.gd moves where the feeler stops while the surface and the name stay the same, and enlarging the second station's visible sphere never stops its feeler. Answer to the doubter: the change-and-run evidence. The stopping place follows the boundary's radius, which the name cannot change. Also acceptable: predicting that giving visible.gd a body and shape would make the feeler stop at the station called Visible. HALF: answers the doubter with reading alone ('solid.gd has a StaticBody3D') or with the run alone ('the feeler stops there'). Or answers the doubter well but says nothing about what looking can or cannot establish. Or answers the doubter only with the debug collision view, which shows where the shape is but not that the test responds to it. MAY LEAVE OUT: the debug view, the label text. WRONG: 'the third sphere looks or behaves heavier'; 'the feeler stops because the sphere is visible or large'; 'you need the collision overlay to know'; agreeing with the doubter.

questions.q: The second station's feeler crosses its sphere. Two classmates want it to stop there too. One plans to edit the feelers' code so that this feeler halts halfway across. The other plans to edit visible.gd. Which plan stays within what this lesson asks you to change, and what else in the study is supplied for you to use rather than change? What would each plan's result tell you about the second sphere? What does this show about why the lesson keeps the feelers exactly as they are?
questions.rubric: FULL: the second plan stays within the lesson. The only files this lesson changes are the three station scripts. Supplied: at least the floor, the light, the camera and the feelers with their movement (the contact test); the station nodes and their labels may also be named. The first plan edits the test itself. The feeler would halt because it was told to, whether or not anything is there; the sphere would still have no boundary, and 'stopped' would no longer be evidence of contact with anything. The second plan gives the second station a boundary (a static body with a collision shape at point_position, joined to the station). The feeler then stops on contact, which shows that the station now has a boundary. Why keep the feelers fixed: a feeler belongs to none of the stations (changing a station's position value does not touch it). It is the one constant test that all three stations meet, so any difference in crossing or stopping comes from what each station built. The lesson's aim is to change what can be crossed, not how crossing happens. With a fixed camera, nothing else moves into the spheres, so the feeler supplies the moving body. HALF: picks the second plan only because 'the lesson says to edit only the three scripts', without saying what the first plan's result would fail to show. Or explains the evidence point but sorts supplied and editable parts wrongly. MAY LEAVE OUT: file names (contact_probe.gd), the keyboard controls, the code for plan two. WRONG: 'plan one is just as good, since the feeler stops either way'; 'make the visible sphere bigger so the feeler stops'; 'the feeler follows point_position'; 'the station scripts create the feelers'; 'the camera or light is yours to change in this lesson'.

questions.q: Every station script builds inside _ready(). What did Point Zero establish about when _ready() runs, and why does that suit building a marker? Now suppose visible.gd's construction were moved, unchanged, into func _process(_delta): (Point Zero's other function) and _ready() removed. Predict what happens when the study runs: what you see, what the scene holds as it keeps running, and what the second station's feeler does. Give reasons.
questions.rubric: Three parts. (1) _ready() runs once, when the node is ready in the scene, not every frame. Built there, each part is made once with .new(), joined to the station with add_child, and stays in the scene after the function ends. (2) _process runs every frame, so every frame makes a new sphere mesh and a new marker and joins it to the station. Nothing removes the old ones, so markers pile up in the same place. The view looks like one sphere, while their number grows every frame without end and the scene costs more and more to run. (3) The feeler still crosses: however many markers there are, they are surfaces only, with nothing to collide with. FULL: all three parts, with reasons. HALF: two of the three. Treating each frame's marker as replacing the last ('it is rebuilt each frame', 'it flickers') counts as missing part (2). MAY LEAVE OUT: -> void, frame rates. WRONG: 'the sphere moves, grows or animates'; '_ready runs every frame'; 'Godot only allows nodes to be made in _ready'; 'the piled-up markers become solid and stop the feeler'.

questions.q: Two classmates explain the stations wrongly. (1) 'The third sphere stops the feeler because the scene lights it. Turn the light off and the feeler would pass through.' (2) 'The second sphere is just too small to stop anything. Make it big enough to fill the feeler's path and the feeler will have to stop.' For each, say what would actually happen and what has been confused. Then say what, in the station scripts, decides whether the feeler stops, and where.
questions.rubric: FULL: (1) Wrong. Light decides how a body is seen, not whether it is met. The museum's wall switch shows this: with the main light off, the long shadows go, a dim fill still shows the spheres, and the collision boundary stays where it was. solid.gd says nothing about light; the light belongs to the supplied scene. With the light off, the feeler would still stop. (2) Wrong. A visible surface of any size gives nothing to collide with. Enlarging visible.gd's radius changes how much the sphere hides, not what can pass through it, and the feeler crosses the bigger sphere. Both confuse how a thing looks with what it is to a moving body. What decides: a physics body (StaticBody3D) placed at the position, with a collision shape attached to it (a SphereShape3D held by a CollisionShape3D that is the body's child), joined to the station. The shape's radius sets where the feeler stops. HALF: only one of the two diagnosed correctly. Or both diagnosed, with nothing on what decides. MAY LEAVE OUT: the dim fill, the shadows, exact class names if the roles are clear. WRONG: 'with the light off, collision is gone'; 'a big enough visible sphere stops the feeler'; 'the station's name, Solid, is what makes it stop'.

questions.q: A hall in the museum holds a sphere built like the third station. There is no feeler there. Describe what a visitor walking up to it experiences in three cases: its boundary is larger than its visible surface, its boundary is smaller, and the two match. What meets the boundary in the museum, and why does the study, with its fixed camera, need feelers at all? What can the hall's maker do by changing one line of the sphere's script?
questions.rubric: FULL: Boundary larger: the visitor is stopped in what looks like empty air before reaching the surface; a gap remains between where they stop and what they see. Boundary smaller: the visitor moves into the white surface (their view or hand passes into it) and is stopped only further in, inside what they see. Matching: the visitor is stopped at the surface. In the museum it is the visitor's own moving body that meets the boundary. The study's camera does not move, so the feeler supplies a moving body that tests the same relation. The maker can change one radius line (the boundary's or the visible one) and so choose whether what is seen and what is met coincide, shaping the encounter. HALF: two of the three cases right, or the two unequal cases swapped. Or the cases right, with nothing on what meets the boundary or on the maker's choice. MAY LEAVE OUT: numbers, the corridor sphere. WRONG: 'the visitor passes through in every case'; 'only the visible size matters to a visitor'; 'the visitor stops at the surface in every case'.

questions.q: In solid.gd, the surface you see and the boundary you meet agree in size and place. What in the script makes them agree, and what makes it possible for them to disagree? And why does the third station repeat the second station's marker before adding its body, instead of having only a body?
questions.rubric: FULL: Agreement: both radii are read from the one radius variable (sphere.radius = radius and sphere_shape.radius = radius), and the marker and the body are both placed at point_position. Nothing else links them. Disagreement is possible because surface and boundary are separate parts held by separate nodes: a mesh shown by a MeshInstance3D, and a shape attached by a CollisionShape3D to a StaticBody3D. Change one of their lines and they part. So whether they coincide is the maker's choice, not something Godot settles. Repeating the marker means the second and third stations look the same, so the only difference between them is the boundary, and the feeler's stop can be put down to the boundary alone. It also puts the boundary beside a surface in one script, where their relation can be chosen and broken. A station with only a body would differ from the second in two ways at once (no surface, and a boundary). HALF: explains the shared radius and the separate parts but not why the marker is repeated, or the reverse. Or says 'that is how Godot works', with no reference to separate parts and a shared value. MAY LEAVE OUT: class names, if the roles are clear. WRONG: 'the body needs a visible marker in order to collide'; 'the marker and the body are one object'; treating a mismatch as a bug to avoid.

questions.q: You want the third station's sphere to sit half a metre higher above the floor than it does now. Write the change to solid.gd. Then predict what you will see and what the third feeler will do. Say how sure you are of each part of your prediction, and why.
questions.rubric: FULL: the edit changes the middle number of point_position's Vector3, which is the height, from 1.12 to 1.62, in that one place (ACCEPT any edit that raises both the marker and the body by 0.5). Certain, from reading the script: the marker and the body are both placed at point_position, so surface and boundary rise together and still match. Not certain from solid.gd: the feeler's path is set by the supplied test, not by point_position, and changing a station's position does not touch it. If the feeler keeps its height (as it did when visible.gd's sphere was raised), it passes beneath the raised sphere and crosses. That is not because the body lost its boundary but because the boundary has left the feeler's path. A conditional answer that names this dependence counts as full. HALF: the right edit, but a confident prediction that the feeler still stops, with no sign of seeing that the script does not set its path. Or the path understood, but the wrong number edited (the first or the third). Or only marker.position raised, which lifts the surface and leaves the boundary behind; half if the student notices the split. WRONG: 'the boundary stays at the old height' after editing point_position; 'the feeler rises with the sphere because it follows the station's point'; raising the sphere by changing the radius.

exam.notes:
I wrote no files and ran no git commands. I did not open any compressed version of the lesson. That includes L2v2.md and _stopped_reconstruction in round2/point-one/, and also the study's own TUTORIAL.md, which may be another telling of the lesson. I read the lesson, the two context files, and, only to check facts in the rubrics, the study's contact_probe.gd, solid.gd, visible.gd, position.gd, study.tscn and CONSTRUCTION.md.

**Changes, by question**

- **Q1 (fault a: rewarded retelling the lesson's order).** The old question asked for a summary of the three stations, which can be copied from the open book. Its rubric also expected a 'baseline' idea the lesson never states, so two judges would score it differently. It now gives a classmate's summary with two natural misconceptions to find: an 'invisible sphere' at the first station, and 'solid instead of visible' at the third. That tests C34, C57, C69 and C118 by diagnosis rather than retelling. 'Baseline' is no longer expected, and where the stations stand in the room is marked not scored.
- **Q2 (faults a and c: the second half rebuilt visible.gd from the open book).** The old second half asked for the parts visible.gd makes, which is a lookup. Q3 already tests those roles by prediction. It now asks why the same edit to the same line shows nothing in position.gd and moves the sphere in visible.gd. That tests what uses a value (C48, C55, C56) against a value alone (C34, C57). The rubric now separates certainty from reading the whole script from certainty from the run alone, which cannot tell a failed edit from a hidden point.
- **Q3 (fault e).** HALF is now defined by count (two of three with reasons, or three with no reasons). Part (c) has a second true reason: the shape would also sit at the station's origin, at floor level. The rubric names it as a plus, and as HALF when it is the only reason given. C23 is added to the claims, because (c) depends on the station being a plain Node3D.
- **Q4 (fault d: the answer leaks).** Listing three combinations gives away the fourth. The rubric now says the naming carries little weight. It also accepts other ways of hiding the marker when the student says why the boundary remains.
- **Q5 (fault e, and a rubric error).** 'Double the visible radius' could mean the radius variable or the sphere.radius line, and the lesson itself calls the variable 'the visible radius'. The question now gives the exact edit, and 'moves both' became 'resizes both'. The old rubric marked any change to sphere.radius WRONG. But sphere.radius = radius - m, with the height kept at twice that, is a correct answer to the spec as worded, so it is now accepted, with HALF if the height line is left stretching the sphere.
- **Q6 (fault e).** 'Which evidence does the lesson actually rest on?' asked about the lesson's telling, and judges would split between 'reading plus running' and 'the intervention'. It is replaced by a doubter who says the test stops at whichever station is called Solid. That has one clear answer: changing only the boundary radius moves the stop while the name stays the same. The debug overlay used as the only answer is HALF.
- **Q7 (faults b and e).** The old FULL answer was a general point about experimental controls, while the lesson's own stated reason ('borrowed equipment'; change what it can cross, not how it moves) earned only HALF. So the rubric rewarded general knowledge and penalised the lesson. It is now a lesson-specific choice between two plans: edit the feeler's code, or edit visible.gd. It asks what each plan's result would say about the sphere, and the rubric credits the lesson's framing alongside the comparison reasoning. The required list of supplied parts is cut to floor, light, camera and feelers; the station nodes and labels are optional.
- **Q8 (fault a).** 'Name one thing left for later' rewarded remembering the lesson's forward pointers (C30 and C31, both detail), so it is dropped. A feeler part is added: piled-up markers still give nothing to collide with, which links the timing question to C64. 'The function the earlier lesson used for counting' was a riddle; it now names _process. 'It is rebuilt each frame' and 'it flickers' are now stated as missing the pile-up part, not as WRONG.
- **Q9 (faults a and d: answered almost word for word in the lesson).** Part (2) said 'paste sun.visible = false into visible.gd', and the lesson's own sentence answers it. Part (1) was close to the lesson's 'the collision boundary stays where it was'. It is now two classmates' wrong theories about the study: 'light makes it stop' carries the museum fact over to the study, and 'a big enough visible sphere would stop it' tests C64. A third part asks what in the scripts decides the stop.
- **Q10 (faults a and d).** 'What does the feeler stand in for?' was nearly a quote of the lesson. The question now asks what meets the boundary in the museum, and why a fixed-camera study needs feelers at all. The matching case is added, so the three cases carry the score.
- **Q11 (faults a, d and e).** The question pointed at one sentence ('the lesson says you have chosen something'), so it rewarded recall. Its premise was also false: the sentence is in the boundary section, not at the end. And its rubric allowed two different answers. It is replaced by a question about why: what in the script makes surface and boundary agree, what lets them disagree, and why the third station repeats the second station's marker (so that the boundary is the only difference between the two).
- **Q12 (fault d).** 'What your prediction depends on that solid.gd does not control' pointed straight at the feeler. It now asks 'how sure are you of each part, and why'. Any edit that raises both the marker and the body by 0.5 is accepted.

**Core and detail marks**

- **C105 moved from core to detail.** 'A reading of the museum source, not a line to paste' is a reading instruction tied to the museum's own code. Its content, that light is separate from the body, is carried by C99 and C102. It cannot be tested without asking the student to repeat the lesson's own warning.
- **C23 moved from detail to core.** That each station script extends a plain Node3D, so the station is not a physics body, is needed to predict Q3(c).
- No other marks changed. C30 and C31 stay detail and no longer appear in any question.

**Coverage**

- All 63 core claims appear in at least one question.
- Vectors: direction 3 (Q1, Q4, Q11), force 4 (Q2, Q6, Q9, Q12), connection 5 (Q3, Q5, Q7, Q8, Q10).
- Code-producing apply questions: Q4 and Q5; Q12 also asks for code.
- Transfer: Q10 and Q12.
- Q8's first sentence draws on earlier content (Point Zero's _ready), as a connect question should. Its score rests on the lesson-specific prediction.

**Facts checked in the study source**

- **Q12:** contact_probe.gd fixes the feeler's height at CENTRE_HEIGHT = 1.12, with a box 0.14 tall. A sphere raised to 1.62 spans 1.48 to 1.76, so the feeler passes underneath. The lesson does not state the feeler's height, so the rubric keeps full credit for a conditional answer.
- **Q6:** the probe stops by physics contact (move_and_collide), not by the station's name, so the doubter is wrong in fact as well as by the lesson's intervention.
- **Q3(c):** a CollisionShape3D under the plain Node3D station gives no boundary, and it would sit at the station's origin.
- **Q8:** CONSTRUCTION.md confirms that nodes built in _ready() stay in the scene after the function ends.

answers.answer: Right: the second sphere can be seen but not met, and the third can be seen and met. Wrong: the first station has no sphere at all, not even an invisible one. position.gd only makes a value, a Vector3 named point_position. It builds no surface, no node and no body, so 'invisible sphere' invents an object that isn't there. The summary also hides that the solid sphere is visible too, because it repeats the visible marker. What each script adds: position.gd gives a location (one number list). visible.gd adds a SphereMesh (a surface description) and a MeshInstance3D that shows it. It gives that node the mesh, puts it at point_position and joins it to the station with add_child, so something appears. solid.gd adds a StaticBody3D at the same position, with a CollisionShape3D holding a SphereShape3D of the same radius, under the body. That gives a boundary the feeler meets. What all three share: extends Node3D, everything built in _ready(), and the same line var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0). What only the first shows: a position is not an object. You can define a location, even change it, and nothing exists there. The other two always put something at the position, so they can't separate 'where' from 'what is there'. The first also shows the feeler is independent equipment: it moves across an empty place no matter what.

In position.gd nothing reads point_position. It is made and then dropped at the end of _ready(), and no node uses it, so changing it changes a number nothing looks at. Nothing is hiding a point, because no point-object was ever made. In visible.gd the line marker.position = point_position hands the value to a node with a visible mesh, so the new value shows as a higher sphere. Can the classmate be sure the edit took effect? Not from the run: nothing visible depends on the value. The grounds come from reasoning, not from seeing. (1) Reading the script shows the value has no reader. (2) The editor's unused-variable warning names exactly that condition. (3) The identical edit in visible.gd visibly works, so the editing and running are fine. So the run's 'nothing' is what we should expect, not a failure. To see the value directly I'd have to make something use it, e.g. print it (if Point Zero's print applies here) or give it a marker.

(a) Without add_child(marker), the marker is built, given its mesh and position, but never joined to the station. It never enters the scene, so nothing appears, and the station looks like the first one. The feeler crosses, as it did before, since visible.gd has no body anyway. (b) Without marker.mesh = sphere, the marker node is placed and added but has no surface. The sphere description is made and never used. Nothing visible appears and the feeler crosses: a node with nothing to show is still just a placed node. (c) solid.add_child(collider) becomes add_child(collider): the shape goes under the station node instead of under the StaticBody3D. The lesson says CollisionShape3D 'attaches that shape to the physics body', so the body now has no shape and nothing gives a boundary. The collider would also sit at the station's origin, since only 'solid' was moved to point_position. I predict the white sphere is still visible (the marker part is untouched) but the feeler now crosses it, like the second station. I'm fairly confident, but the lesson doesn't say outright what a shape does when it isn't under a body.

Missing combination: cannot be seen, but stops the feeler (invisible but solid). Edit solid.gd by deleting the line add_child(marker), or the whole marker block. The script becomes: extends Node3D / func _ready() -> void: / var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0) / var radius := 0.14 / var solid := StaticBody3D.new() / solid.position = point_position / var sphere_shape := SphereShape3D.new() / sphere_shape.radius = radius / var collider := CollisionShape3D.new() / collider.shape = sphere_shape / solid.add_child(collider) / add_child(solid). Point Zero, as restated here: _ready() runs when the scene is ready, at the start and (I understand) once. That suits building a marker: you build the sphere once, at the moment the station enters the scene, and it then just stays there. If the same construction ran in _process(_delta) instead (I take Point Zero's other function to run every frame, again and again): each frame would make a new SphereMesh and a new MeshInstance3D at the same position and add it to the station. You would see one white sphere, because all the copies are identical and sit exactly on top of each other. But the scene would keep piling up new marker nodes, one per frame, thousands within a minute, and would probably slow down as it runs. (1) Light doesn't make a boundary. The lesson's museum switch turns off the sun: the shadows go, the spheres stay dimly visible, and 'the collision boundary stays where it was'. With the light off, the third feeler would still stop. Also the second sphere is lit just the same and the feeler crosses it, so light can't be what stops things. The lesson grows the second sphere to radius 0.3 and the feeler still crosses it. Making it fill the whole path would hide more but stop nothing. This confuses the mesh (surface) with a collision shape. What decides it, in solid.gd only: var solid := StaticBody3D.new(), a body that takes part in collision; a SphereShape3D whose radius sets the boundary's size (sphere_shape.radius = radius); collider.shape = sphere_shape; solid.add_child(collider), which puts the shape under the body; solid.position = point_position, which sets where it is; and add_child(solid), which puts it in the scene. visible.gd has none of these lines, so its feeler passes.

In the museum it's your own movement that meets the boundary. Boundary larger than the surface: the visitor is stopped before reaching the white surface, held back by empty air at a gap, as if the sphere had an invisible shell. Boundary smaller: the visitor walks into the white surface and partly inside it before being stopped, so what you see swallows you before anything resists. Matching: you are stopped exactly where you see the surface, and seeing and touching agree. The study's camera is fixed and never moves, so nothing of 'you' can bump into the sphere there. They agree because the script hands both the same values. Size: sphere.radius = radius and sphere_shape.radius = radius. Place: marker.position = point_position and solid.position = point_position. They can disagree because they are two separate objects, a MeshInstance3D with a SphereMesh (what you see) and a StaticBody3D with a SphereShape3D (what you meet). Each has its own radius and position, and nothing links them except the script choosing to give them the same numbers. Change one line (e.g. sphere_shape.radius = 0.35) and they separate. Why repeat the marker: a body alone is invisible, so the station would show 'solid but unseen', not a visible sphere that also stops things. Building the second station's marker unchanged and only adding the body also makes the comparison clean. Station two and station three differ by exactly the added body, so the feeler's stop can be credited to that addition alone.

answers.answer: Right: the second sphere can be seen but not met, and the third can be seen and met. Wrong: the first station has no invisible sphere. It has no sphere at all. position.gd only makes a Vector3 value named point_position. No node, no surface and no boundary are added to the scene, and nothing ever uses the value. It is a place, and a point has no size. Each station adds something new. visible.gd adds a SphereMesh (the surface), a MeshInstance3D (the node that shows it), sets its position and joins it with add_child. solid.gd builds that same marker and then adds a StaticBody3D with a CollisionShape3D holding a SphereShape3D (the boundary). So the third is not one 'solid sphere' but two parts that happen to agree in place and size. All three scripts share extends Node3D, building inside _ready(), and the same point_position Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0). The second and third also share radius 0.14 and the marker code. What only the first station can show: a position and an object placed there are different things. Writing down a place makes nothing exist there, so nothing appears and nothing resists. Stations 2 and 3 always put a body at the place, so on their own they could not pull the place apart from the thing.

In position.gd, point_position is set and never read. No line uses it to place anything, so changing 1.12 to 1.7 changes a number that nothing looks at. Nothing appeared before the edit and nothing appears after it, and nothing is hiding a point, because there is no body to show. In visible.gd the line marker.position = point_position reads the value and places the marker. The same edit therefore moves the sphere. How sure can we be that the edit took effect? Not from looking: the screen is the same either way. The grounds are indirect. (1) Reading the script shows nothing uses the variable, so no visible change is the expected result. (2) The editor's unused-variable warning names exactly that. (3) The same save-and-run steps visibly work in visible.gd, so the workflow is sound. That is fairly strong reasoning but not direct observation. To see it directly you would have to make something read the value, for example showing it on a label as Point Zero did with str().

(a) Delete add_child(marker): the sphere and marker are still created, and the marker's mesh and position are still set, but the marker is never joined to the station, so it is not in the scene. Nothing appears at the second station; it looks like the first. The feeler crosses, as it already did. (b) Delete marker.mesh = sphere: the marker node is added at point_position but has no surface, so nothing shows. The SphereMesh is built and left unused. The feeler crosses. Either way the station shows nothing, but in (b) an empty node sits in the scene, while in (a) the node exists only in the script and never joins it. (c) In solid.gd, add_child(collider) instead of solid.add_child(collider): the shape is no longer under the StaticBody3D. It becomes a child of the station, at the station's own origin rather than 1.12 up (only solid was given point_position). The lesson says CollisionShape3D attaches its shape to the physics body by being its child, so now the body has no shape and the shape has no body. My prediction: the white sphere still shows, and the third feeler crosses it like the second one does. I am reasoning from the lesson's description, not from having seen it.

Change one line:  sphere_shape.radius = radius + 0.05   (0.05 is the margin and can be any fixed amount). Then set var radius := 0.28 and run. Centre: unchanged, still point_position, because neither the marker's nor the body's position depends on radius. Visible size: the sphere doubles, to radius 0.28 and height 0.56, since height is radius * 2.0. Feeler: it stops 0.33 from the centre, earlier than before, still leaving the same small 0.05 gap in front of the white surface. Why one edit resizes both: the surface (sphere.radius = radius) and the boundary (sphere_shape.radius = radius + 0.05) are both computed from the same variable. Change it once and every line that reads it follows, the same way height followed radius in the lesson. This assumes the feeler travels through the sphere's height, as it does now.

Looking: shows both have a white surface of the same size in the same place. It cannot show solidity, because the lesson shows a surface gives nothing to collide with. Running: the third feeler stops and its contact label says stopped; the second feeler crosses. That shows something at the third station stops the feeler and nothing at the second does. It cannot show what does the stopping, or that it is tied to the sphere rather than to the test. The Visible Collision Shapes overlay adds a picture of a shape at the third station only. Reading: solid.gd has StaticBody3D + SphereShape3D + CollisionShape3D, and visible.gd has none of them. That shows how they are built differently. It cannot prove the running scene does what the text says (an unsaved edit, the wrong script attached, a feeler that ignores collision). Changing and rerunning: set sphere_shape.radius = 0.35 and the feeler stops earlier with a gap; set 0.07 (with radius 0.3) and it sinks into the surface. That shows cause: the stopping point follows the boundary line in solid.gd. It still only proves the one thing you varied. The doubter is answered by changing and rerunning. A rule that stops at whatever station is called 'Solid' could not make the stop move closer or farther when only sphere_shape.radius changes; the name stayed the same and the stop moved. Editing visible.gd stays within the lesson: position.gd, visible.gd and solid.gd are 'the three scripts we will change'. Supplied for use: contact_probe.gd (the feelers' movement, 'borrowed equipment, like the camera'), the camera, floor, light, the labels and the study scene. Plan 1 (making the feeler halt halfway): the feeler would stop, but that would tell you nothing about the sphere, which would still have no boundary. The stop would come from a rule written into the instrument, a staged result. Plan 2 (adding a StaticBody3D with a CollisionShape3D to visible.gd): if the feeler stops, that is real evidence that the second sphere now has a boundary, and where it stops shows the boundary's size. Point Zero: _ready() runs once, when the node and its children are in the scene tree, not every frame. Moving the count into it gave one, and it stayed at one. That suits building a marker: you build it once, it joins the scene, and it stays. Moved into _process(_delta): Godot calls _process every frame, so every frame the script makes a new SphereMesh and a new MeshInstance3D and adds it. You would still see one white sphere at the same place, because the copies are identical and stacked on top of each other, so they look like one. The scene would hold a growing pile of marker children, one more per frame, like Point Zero's count climbing. Over time that may slow the study down; that last part is my guess. The second feeler still crosses: none of the copies has a collision body, so a hundred surfaces stop no more than one.

(1) Light: turning the light off (the museum's sun.visible = false) removes the long shadows. A dim fill keeps the spheres visible, and the lesson says the collision boundary stays where it was. The feeler would still stop. This mixes up how a thing is seen (light, surface) with whether it can be met (the boundary). (2) Size: the lesson tried this. With radius 0.3 in visible.gd the sphere is bigger and the feeler still crosses. A visible surface has no boundary at any size. Equally, the third station still stops the feeler when its boundary is only 0.07. This mixes up the size of the surface with having a boundary at all. What decides it: in solid.gd only, the StaticBody3D (var solid := StaticBody3D.new(), joined with add_child(solid)) with a CollisionShape3D child (solid.add_child(collider)) whose shape is a SphereShape3D. Where the feeler stops is set by sphere_shape.radius around solid.position = point_position. The marker lines have no say.

In the museum the visitor's own movement meets the boundary, through the supplied player. Boundary larger than the surface: the visitor is stopped before reaching the white surface, held back by empty space, and can never quite touch it. Boundary smaller: the visitor pushes into the visible surface, so the white swallows the view or hand, and is stopped only partway inside. Matching: the visitor is stopped exactly at the surface, and the sphere feels solid where it looks solid. The study runs on the desktop base with a fixed camera and no player, no walking and no hands. Nothing of yours moves there, so the feeler is a supplied moving body standing in for your movement, to test the same relation. The hall's maker, by changing the one line sphere_shape.radius, decides whether seeing and meeting agree, or opens a gap, or lets the visitor sink in. That is a design choice about the encounter, not just about appearance. Exactly how a walking body or a VR hand meets a sphere at about 1.12 m is beyond what the lesson shows.

Agreement: both parts read the same two variables. marker.position and solid.position are both set from point_position, and sphere.radius and sphere_shape.radius are both set from radius. Disagreement is possible because they are separate objects with separate settings: a SphereMesh for the surface and a SphereShape3D for the boundary, each with its own radius, and each node with its own position. Write a different value into one line (0.35, 0.07) and they come apart; nothing joins them except the shared variables. Why repeat the marker: a body alone draws nothing, so the station would be invisible (the Q4 combination). To compare with station 2, station 3 must look exactly the same, so the only difference between them is the added boundary. Each station adds one thing to the one before, so any difference in the feeler's behaviour can be put down to that one addition.

Change the first line of solid.gd to:  var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.62, 0.0)   (y is up; 1.12 + 0.5). Because the marker and the body both take their position from point_position, the sphere and its boundary rise together. Predictions: (1) The white sphere appears half a metre higher, same size. Sure: the lesson showed 1.7 raising the sphere in visible.gd, and the taxonomy says y is how far up. (2) The boundary moves up with it, still matching the surface. Sure, from reading the script. If the feeler sweeps along the old height, about 1.12, it would now pass under a boundary whose bottom sits at about 1.48 and cross without stopping. If the feeler is set to follow the sphere's height, it would still stop. Not sure; I would run it to find out. O-ctx.teach_back: This lesson is about the fact that a 'thing' in a 3D scene is really several separate decisions. A place is just numbers; nothing exists there until you build something. The feelers let us test what can be met while the camera stays fixed. In the museum, it's your own body that runs into these choices. It leads on to Point Coordinates, where the three numbers of a position become the subject, and then to two positions for a line. Making things starts with knowing what you actually placed.

From this lesson: _ready() runs once, as the node starts in the scene. That suits a marker: you want it built a single time, and then it stays. There is only a position: a Vector3 held in a variable that nothing uses. No body, no size, nothing at all is in the scene there. Second, 'a visible one and a solid one' makes them sound like opposites. The solid one is visible too, and the visible one is not solid. What each script makes: position.gd makes only point_position, three numbers. visible.gd adds a SphereMesh (what is seen) and a MeshInstance3D marker that shows it, placed at point_position and added to the scene with add_child. solid.gd keeps that marker and adds a StaticBody3D at the same position, with a CollisionShape3D holding a SphereShape3D of the same radius (what is touched). A point has a place but no size, so nothing is seen and nothing stops the feeler. It is also the control: the feeler crosses when nothing is there at all. Point Zero: _ready() runs once, when the node and its children are in the scene tree, not every frame. Moving the counter into _ready gave one, and it stayed at one. That suits a marker: you want it built once at the start, and it then stays. If the construction moved into _process(_delta), it would run every frame, like count += 1 did. Each frame would make a new SphereMesh and a new marker and add_child it at the same position. (2) Making the second sphere big: setting radius to 0.3 just makes it grow with the same centre, and the feeler still crosses, passing hidden inside it. However big it gets, a mesh has no boundary. What decides it: in solid.gd, the StaticBody3D with a CollisionShape3D child holding a SphereShape3D (solid.add_child(collider), then add_child(solid)). Where the feeler stops is set by sphere_shape.radius and solid.position = point_position.

In the museum, what meets the boundary is your own movement: the visitor's supplied player body. Boundary larger: you are stopped before you reach the white surface, by a gap of empty air you cannot pass, as if it had an invisible skin. Boundary smaller: you walk partway into the white sphere before anything stops you. Your view may push into the surface, as the feeler sinks in at the study. Boundaries match: you stop where the surface is, and it feels like a solid ball. The study has a fixed camera and no walking player, so nothing would move into the shape. The feeler is a supplied moving body standing in for the visitor, so the encounter can be seen at all. By changing one line, sphere_shape.radius, the hall's maker chooses whether the seen and the met coincide. They can make the sphere guard more space than it shows, let people sink into it, or make it honest. That is the 'another way to change the encounter' the corridor's large sphere points to. They agree because the same variables feed both. sphere.radius = radius and sphere_shape.radius = radius give the same size, and marker.position = point_position and solid.position = point_position give the same place. They can disagree because they are two separate things built by separate lines: the mesh on a MeshInstance3D, and the shape in a CollisionShape3D under a StaticBody3D. Nothing ties them together except that both lines read the same variables. Write a different number on one line and they part. The third station repeats the marker because a body with a shape is not seen. Without the marker you would get the invisible solid from Q4, not a sphere you can both see and meet. Change the first line of solid.gd to var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.62, 0.0), adding 0.5 to the middle number, which is y, up. Both marker.position and solid.position read point_position, so the mesh and the shape move up together. Prediction for what I see: the white sphere sits half a metre higher. I am confident of this, because the code moves it and visible.gd's 1.7 test showed the sphere rising. Prediction for the feeler: I am not sure. The lesson never says at what height the feelers travel or how big they are. If a feeler's path is fixed near the old height, the shape now spans about 1.48 to 1.76, so the feeler passes under it and crosses. If the feeler moves at the sphere's height, it stops as before. It leads into the museum, where your own walking body meets these shapes, as with the large sphere ending the corridor. questions.q: (a) Describe the stair as a body: what one row of it is, where each row comes from, and what it means that one row stands further back and higher than another. (b) The 4 x 4 grid of chapter 3 was also built by a loop. In what way is the stair a different kind of body? (c) The step keeps only two rows of bytes and reuses them at every step. Where, then, does the stair keep all of its rows? (d) The next stop builds a tree with a function that calls itself, and it has no grid of cells. Which idea of this chapter does it keep, and which parts of this chapter's machinery does it no longer need?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d) all right. HALF = (a) right and two of (b) to (d) right. A MISUNDERSTANDING in (a) scores zero. (a) A row is the state of the whole line of cells at one step, each cell on or off. Row 0 is a chosen start (one live cell, the seed). Every later row is computed from the row just before it by the same rule, applied to every cell. Further back and higher both mean later, so walking up the stair is walking forward through the steps of the computation. (b) In the grid each copy's place came from its own address alone: no copy depended on another, and they could be made in any order. In the stair each row depends on the one before, so the rows can only be made in order. The body is the record (the history) of a process, not a shape placed part by part. (c) At each step lay_row() builds a new row node from the buffer's current bytes (its tiles, and later its colliders) and adds it to the scene. The bytes are overwritten afterwards, but the nodes stay. The history lives in the scene's nodes, not in the arrays. (d) Kept: a rule applied to its own result, so what one step produces is what the next step works on. No longer needed: the grid of cells and its neighbourhood, and with them the choice of edges. Whether the two buffers survive is not graded; a reason either way is welcome. A strong answer notes that the buffers exist because many cells are updated from one shared old row, which a chain of calls does not have. MAY LEAVE OUT: sizes, the number of rows, the pace, rule numbers, the name of the fractal. MISUNDERSTANDING: rows computed independently of each other (from their own index, or at random); the author choosing each row; height standing for a cell's value instead of time; the history kept in the arrays; the next stop keeping the grid or the neighbours.

questions.q: Invent a rule the lesson does not use: a cell is alive in the next row exactly when its LEFT neighbour is alive in this row, whatever the cell itself and its right neighbour are. (a) What is this rule's number? Show how you got it. (b) A cell's left, self and right are 1, 0, 1. Work through what the lesson's step computes for this cell with your rule number, and say whether the cell is alive next. (c) Start from one live cell in the middle of the row. Describe the floor this rule builds over many rows, first with the ends joined, then with every cell beyond an end dead.
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a), (b) and both cases of (c). HALF = the method right with one arithmetic slip, or (c) missing a case or giving the wrong direction. (a) 240. The eight patterns are numbered from 111 (7) down to 000 (0). The four with left = 1 (patterns 7, 6, 5, 4) answer 1 and the other four answer 0. With pattern 7 as the highest binary digit, the answers read 11110000 = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = 240. (b) index = 1*4 + 0*2 + 1 = 5. 240 >> 5 = 7 (binary 111), and 7 & 1 = 1, so the cell is alive, as the rule says (its left neighbour is alive). (c) Each cell copies its left neighbour, so the one live cell moves one cell to the right (toward the higher index) with every row: a diagonal line of single tiles running back, up and to the right. It never grows or splits. With the ends joined it reaches the right end and comes back in at the left end. With dead ends it walks off the right end, and every row after that is empty. MAY LEAVE OUT: whether the floor can be walked. MISUNDERSTANDING: 15 (the answers read with pattern 0 as the highest digit, so the link between a pattern's number and its digit's place is missing; with 15, part (b) gives 0, dead, which contradicts the rule); 4 (the live answers counted instead of placed); calling the number an arbitrary label; predicting a spreading triangle; in (b), indexing the rule by the cell's position instead of by its pattern.

questions.q: A student writes this step for the stair (Rule 90, 17 cells, ends joined, one live cell in the middle): `for k in n:` then, indented, `var i := n - 1 - k` (the loop runs from the last cell down to the first), `var index := now[(i - 1 + n) % n] * 4 + now[i] * 2 + now[(i + 1) % n]` and `now[i] = (rule >> index) & 1`. (a) Before it runs, what will row 1 be? Say at which cell the first wrong value appears, and why the error does not stay in that cell. (b) Which way will the floor lean, and what decides that? (c) What made a floor that is the same on both sides of the middle the right thing to expect from this rule and this start? (d) Godot will print no error and no warning. What does that tell you about how a fault like this is found, and what will you ask first the next time a floor leans?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d), with the first wrong cell and the direction right. Row 1 exactly as below is expected; a trace with one slip after the first wrong cell still counts if the mechanism and the direction are right. HALF = names writing into the row being read as the fault, but misplaces the first wrong cell or gets the direction wrong (for example 'leans right', copied from the lesson's left-to-right version); or (a) to (c) right and (d) only 'debug it'. (a) Row 1: cells 0 to 9 alive, cells 10 to 16 dead. The fault is that each answer is written into the same array the loop is still reading. Cells 16 down to 9 come out right: the right neighbours they read were rewritten, but to the values they already had, and cell 9 reads the old seed. The first wrong value is cell 8, the seed's own cell. Its right neighbour, cell 9, has already been rewritten to 1, so it answers 1 where the old row gives 0. Each wrong answer is the right neighbour of the next cell the loop visits, so the error runs on to cell 0 in a single step. (b) Toward index 0, the left side of the stair: the end the loop runs toward. (c) Rule 90 gives a pattern and its mirror image the same answer, the seed is in the middle, and the ring has no favoured side. Nothing in the rule or the start can tell left from right, so any lean must come from how the step is computed. (d) The code is legal and does exactly what it says. A fault of this kind gives no error, only a wrong result, so it is found by predicting the result before running and comparing. The first question: which row was the rule reading, the old row or one already partly rewritten? Any paraphrase counts. MAY LEAVE OUT: how many cells differ from their mirror. MISUNDERSTANDING: blaming the wrap (%), integer division, the drawing, the rule number or Godot; thinking the error stays in one cell or is random; thinking a symmetric floor needed luck; thinking errors always run to the right.

questions.q: Widen the neighbourhood: a cell's next state now depends on five cells of the row before, itself and two on each side. (a) Write step() for it, with the lesson's two arrays and the ends joined, and say what else in the script must change, and why. (b) Back in the lesson's own three-cell stair at Rule 90, predict the floor, with a reason, for each of these changes: (i) in _ready(), `next = now` in place of `next.resize(n)`; (ii) in _ready(), `next = now.duplicate()` in place of `next.resize(n)`; (iii) the three swap lines at the end of step() deleted; (iv) the three swap lines replaced by the single line `now = next`.
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) correct, with the swap after the loop and the range change named, and all four predictions with reasons. HALF = (a) correct and two or three predictions right; or all four predictions right and the code with a slip in the weights. (a) Code of this shape: for i in n: var index := cell_at(i - 2) * 16 + cell_at(i - 1) * 8 + now[i] * 4 + cell_at(i + 1) * 2 + cell_at(i + 2) (or wrapped with % directly); next[i] = (rule >> index) & 1. After the loop: var spare := now; now = next; next = spare. Every neighbour is read from now, every answer is written to next, and the swap comes after the loop. The weights must be distinct powers of two, so each of the 32 patterns gets its own number from 0 to 31 (any consistent order, stated). To change: 32 patterns need a 32-digit binary number, so the export range of 0 to 255 must allow up to 2^32 - 1. Noting that cell_at already handles indices two beyond an end is welcome. (b)(i) '=' gives the same bytes a second name. The step writes into the row it reads, and the leaning floor of the first version comes back from row 1 on. (ii) A copy has its own bytes. Its starting contents do not matter, because every cell of next is written before anything reads it, so the floor is right (Sierpinski's triangle). (iii) The answers go into next and nobody reads them. now never changes, so every row is the seed: one tile per row. (iv) Row 1 is right, since it was read from one array and written to the other. After `now = next` both names hold the same bytes, so from the second step on the step reads and writes one array. From row 2 on the floor is wrong, as in the first version, and no longer the same on both sides. MAY LEAVE OUT: exact export syntax; a separate edge function, if they wrap with %. MISUNDERSTANDING: reading some neighbours from next; putting the swap inside the loop (not even HALF for (a), even if the code otherwise runs); believing that '=' or the swap copies bytes; believing a duplicated next breaks the stair because it starts with the seed; 10 or 25 patterns.

questions.q: The rule gives every cell a left and a right neighbour, but a row has two ends. (a) What does the stair do at its ends by default, and how does its neighbour lookup do it? (b) Add a third ending: beyond each end, the row continues with a copy of its own end cell. Change the lookup function, and the setting that chooses the ending, to offer it. (c) Before running: on which rows can a floor with your new ending differ from the default floor, and why only there? (d) Which ending belongs to the rule itself? What is gained by making the ending a setting you switch, instead of leaving one built in?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d). HALF = the code right but (c) saying the floors differ everywhere or from the first row; or (d) naming one ending as the rule's own; the rest right. (a) The ends are joined into a ring. The remainder % turns index -1 into the last cell and index n into the first, so a cell at one end has the other end's cell as its neighbour. (b) Any working form. Replace the bool with a choice of three (an int, a string or an enum). In the lookup, every choice returns now[i] inside the row. Beyond an end: ring returns now[(i + n) % n]; copy returns now[0] for i < 0 and now[n - 1] for i >= n (or now[clamp(i, 0, n - 1)]); dead returns 0. (c) Only from the row after a live cell first reaches an end cell, and only near the border. Until then the end cells are dead, so every ending finds a dead cell beyond the end, and all endings make the same rows. (d) None of them. The rule is defined on a row without ends, which no machine has. A grid has to end somewhere, and how it ends is the author's decision. As a setting, the choice becomes visible and testable instead of a default nobody noticed. MAY LEAVE OUT: Godot's clamp; that copy and ring agree on floors that are the same on both sides (a strong answer may notice it). MISUNDERSTANDING: % seen only as a guard against a crash; the dead end or the ring taken as the real behaviour; the ending changing the rule; the ending mattering in every row.

questions.q: (a) In the first finished stair every tile is drawn, yet the walker walks through them on the ground. Why? (b) In the version where each row gets a body, a student writes the loop over a row's cells as `for i in n:` in place of the lesson's `for i in n + 1:`. Everything else is as in the lesson. Which tiles now fail to hold the walker, in which rows, and why? (c) Take a row of eight cells: 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 1. How many boxes does the lesson's loop make, how many cells wide is each, and at which value of i is each one made?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (c). HALF = (b) or (c) partly right as described below, the rest right. (a) The tiles are a MultiMesh: drawn to be seen, with no shape, so nothing stops the walker. (b) A box is made only when a run of live cells is closed, either by the first dead cell after it or by the extra pass at i = n. Without that pass, a run that reaches the last cell is never closed. In every row whose last cell is alive, the whole run ending at the right edge is drawn but has no box, and the walker falls through it. All other runs keep their boxes. HALF for (b): 'the last tile gets no collider', without the whole run or without saying which rows. (c) Two boxes. One is three cells wide (cells 1 to 3), made at i = 4, the first dead cell after the run. The other is two cells wide (cells 6 and 7), made only at i = 8, the extra pass. HALF for (c): the runs right but the moment the second box is made missed. MAY LEAVE OUT: box positions. MISUNDERSTANDING: (a) the tiles are too thin or the walker too big; (b) the last tile is not drawn; (c) five boxes (one per live cell), or one box for all the live cells.

questions.q: After comparing four rules, each from one live cell, the lesson makes a claim about what an eight-answer rule decides and what its number does not tell you. (a) State the claim in your own words. (b) How was it established? (c) Two of the pairs compared each differ in two of their eight answers. What did the comparison show about those two pairs? From how the step works, why is it reasonable that counting the answers that differ does not predict how alike two floors will be? (d) The two floors that look most alike: why are they so alike, in terms of their cells? (e) How far does the claim reach? Say what it was measured on, and what you would have to run before saying it holds for floors in general.
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (e). HALF = (a) and (b) right and two of (c) to (e), with no misunderstanding. (a) The eight answers fix the floor completely, and they decide between kinds as different as a regular checker, a fractal, a lopsided growth and a disorder. Yet the number, or its digits, does not say which kind you will get. (b) By prediction and experiment: a prediction was written first, then each rule was run from the same start and the floors were measured (stills compared, cells counted). It was not derived from the tables. (c) The two pairs were far from equally alike: in the lesson one pair differed on about one and a half times as many cells as the other, and a pair four answers apart was closer than pairs three apart. Any one reason: an answer matters only where its pattern of three actually occurs, and which patterns occur, and how often, depends on the history each rule makes; or each row is made from the last, so one changed cell changes the next row's neighbourhoods, and a difference can spread or stay small. HALF for (c): the measured break without a reason, or a reason without the break. (d) Every live cell of one floor (Rule 90) is also live in the other (Rule 250). The checker is the fractal with its holes filled, so the two differ only on the holes. A remark on why (250 makes a cell alive when either neighbour is, 90 when exactly one is) is welcome but not required. (e) One live cell in the middle, a short row on a ring, eleven rows. Other starts, widths, numbers of rows and endings are not shown; to say more, run them and count again. The claim is an observed result, not a proof. A mention that the lesson counted two other floors without rendering (dead ends; a wider ring with more rows) and the same pair stayed closest is welcome. MAY LEAVE OUT: the percentages, the cell counts, the views of the stills, which rules form the pairs in (c). MISUNDERSTANDING: 'the rule number predicts the look'; 'fewer differing answers means more alike'; 'derived from the tables'; treating the claim as proven in general.

questions.q: A classmate is choosing a floor for the walkway of their room. They argue three things from the sheet of four rules and the process strip. 1: 'Rules 90 and 250 differ on only about 8% of the picture, the closest pair, so for my walkway they are interchangeable.' 2: 'The step that gave every row its colliders changed the picture by 0.00%, so it changed nothing and I can leave it out.' 3: 'The faulty one-array step changed the picture by 14.5% and the repair by 13.3%, so the repair is nearly as big a mistake as the fault.' For each claim, say what is wrong with it and why. Then say how you would find out whether a floor will hold a visitor of a given size.
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = all three claims answered with reasons, plus a test with a body. HALF = two claims with reasons plus the test, or all three without the test. 1: Likeness in a picture is not likeness for a body. The two floors differ exactly on the holes (every tile of 90 is also a tile of 250). The holes are small in a picture, but they decide whether a body smaller than a cell falls through: a marble dropped over the middle of row 4 fell through 90 and stayed on 250. Whether the floors are interchangeable depends on the body's size against the gaps: the walker, wider than a gap, was stopped at the seed on both. Any argument from hole size against body size counts. An answer that only says '250 is walkable and 90 is not' is not enough for this claim. 2: Colliders are touched, not seen. A row without them looks the same, but the walker walks through it. That step changed the body completely and the picture not at all. 3: How much a picture changes says nothing about right or wrong. The repair is a large change because it undoes a large error. Correctness is judged against a prediction (row 1 two cells, the floor the same on both sides), not by the size of a change. TEST: put a body on the floor (drop an object, send the walker) and read where it ends up (its height; arrived, fell or stopped); compare runs and gaps with the body's width; change a size, such as the cell against the body, and test again. MAY LEAVE OUT: the particular results for the walker and the marble; any argument from understanding is as good as the lesson's examples. MISUNDERSTANDING: 'a better camera would settle it'; 'if it looks solid it is solid'; agreeing with claim 3.

questions.q: The orange pool looks nothing like the stair. (a) In idea, what does its step share with the stair's step? (b) What is different about what a cell holds, and about the rule? (c) The 24 x 24 floor lies in one array, row after row. Given only a cell's index i and the width g, write the index of its right neighbour and of its back neighbour (the row before), both with the floor's edges joined. Why is i + 1 not always the right neighbour? (d) Why does each substance need two arrays? If each new value were written straight back into its own array, toward which side would the pattern be pushed, and why that side?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d). HALF = three of the four right, with no misunderstanding. (a) New values are computed only from the old arrays and written into separate ones, and the names are swapped afterwards, for both substances. Neighbours are found by index, with % joining opposite edges. (b) A cell holds two amounts (of A and of B), not one on/off bit. The rule is a formula, not a table of eight answers: each amount moves toward the mean of its four neighbours, with B slower than A, and B is made from A where both are present, A fed in and B taken out. Any fair statement of spreading plus reaction counts; the coefficients are not needed. (c) x = i % g and z = i / g (whole-number division). Right = z * g + (x + 1) % g, or i - x + (x + 1) % g. Back = (i - g + g * g) % (g * g), or (z - 1 + g) % g * g + x. At the end of a row (x = g - 1), i + 1 is the first cell of the next row, not the first cell of this row. (d) Written in place, a cell's left and back neighbours, visited earlier by the loops, would already be new, so each cell would read a mix of old and new values. The error would be carried the way the loops run, toward higher x and higher z, and the square pattern would skew that way. Noting that B's update would also read A's new value is welcome. MAY LEAVE OUT: the coefficients, the feed and kill values, the history of the model. MISUNDERSTANDING: cells on or off as in the stair; neighbours as all eight cells around; % only to avoid an index error; the pool as random; i + 1 taken as the right neighbour everywhere.

questions.q: Rule 30's floor looks disordered, and its middle column has been used as a source of random numbers. (a) Is there any chance in it? Give a reason from the step's code, and say what you would run to check. (b) Connect this to what the course taught about seeds: what does someone hold who has the rule and the first row? (c) A classmate wants a 'truly random' stair. They fill the first row with randi_range(0, 1) from a RandomNumberGenerator with a fixed seed, then run Rule 30. Is the floor now random? What decides it, and what will two runs give? (d) Does the orange pool behave the same way? Give a reason from its step.
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d). HALF = three of the four; or (b) given only as 'pseudo-random', without saying that the rule and the first row act as the seed. (a) No chance. The step reads only the old row and the rule number and does fixed arithmetic. It draws no random number, so the same start gives the same rows. Check: run it twice and compare the printed rows (the lesson did; the middle column matched). (b) The rule and the first row act as a seed. Whoever has them can produce every 'random' number in advance, as often as they like. (c) Only the first row was drawn, and with a fixed seed the draws repeat, so the seed and the rule decide the whole floor and two runs give the same floor. A new seed gives a new floor, but the chance is all in the first row, never in the step. (d) Yes. Its step is fixed arithmetic on the old arrays with fixed feed and kill, and draws nothing, so two pools from the same start match (the lesson ran two side by side and they matched to the last digit). MAY LEAVE OUT: the column's digits; the history of its use. MISUNDERSTANDING: Rule 30 uses a random function; disorder means chance; different runs give different floors; in (c), the floor is random because the first row was drawn; the pool's organic look means randomness.

questions.q: The orange pool holds the walker up. (a) The pool's step only changes numbers in arrays. What in the kit turns those numbers into something that holds the walker up? (b) Who decided those things, and could they have been decided otherwise? (c) Name decisions of the same kind in the stair: things the rule does not contain, but the floor depends on. (d) A visitor says of your stair: 'Nobody designed this; the rule made it.' What is right in that, and what does it leave out?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (d). HALF = (a) naming only the collider, or (c) listing decisions without saying the rule does not contain them; the rest right. (a) A supplied line hands B's amounts to a collider (one height for each cell), and a threshold, a tenth, below which a cell counts as nothing. The pattern alone is numbers in arrays. (b) The author decided both. Another threshold, another way of turning numbers into a body, or no body at all were all possible; nothing in the reaction asks for them. (c) Any two or more: where the row ends and what lies beyond it (ring or dead); the seed (one live cell, in the middle); what counts as there (a 1 becomes a tile and part of a box); the cell size and the rise against the walker's size; how many rows; one box for each run. (d) Right: once the rule, the start and the edges are set, no one places a tile, and each row follows from the last. Left out: who set them. The rule, the edge, the seed, the sizes and what counts as present were chosen, and the floor depends on every one of them. Credit the pattern only with what it does. MAY LEAVE OUT: the threshold's value; Turing and Gray-Scott; the larger question the lesson leaves open. MISUNDERSTANDING: the equations themselves make the floor solid; the rule fixes the edge or the seed; the pattern is objective, so nobody decided anything; or the opposite, that the author designed every row.

questions.q: (a) What does the stair's clock do each frame, and why does it keep the time left over after a step instead of setting itself back to zero? (b) Change _process so that if one frame lasts a long time (a stall of a whole second, say), every row that is owed is laid in that same frame, but never more rows than the stair keeps. (c) Laying every row before the first frame and laying them one by one give the same floor. Why, and what does the pacing add?
questions.rubric: GRADE: FULL = (a) to (c). HALF = (b) without the made < rows bound, or with the clock reset to zero; or (a) giving the mechanics but no reason for keeping the remainder; the rest right. (a) Each frame it adds delta, the seconds since the last frame, to a running total. When the total reaches the pace it takes one step, lays one row and subtracts the pace. Keeping the remainder keeps the rows on schedule on average at any frame rate. Resetting to zero would throw that time away, and the stair would run slow by an amount that depends on the machine. A strong answer notes that with the lesson's if, the rows owed after a stall arrive one per frame over the next frames. (b) Keep the early return for pace <= 0 or made >= rows; then clock += delta; then while clock >= pace and made < rows: clock -= pace; step(); lay_row(). (c) Each row depends only on the row before and the rule, not on when it is computed, so the floor is the same. Pacing turns the order of computation into arrival in time, which each row's place (further back, higher) then records. MAY LEAVE OUT: the exact syntax of the guard. MISUNDERSTANDING: multiplying the pace by delta; assuming every frame lasts the same; thinking a faster pace changes the pattern.
